title: Cities that never sleep?
text: Night-time economies have become a measure of urban {{1}}, and cities compete to advertise how much happens after dark. Yet researchers studying night workers tell a more complicated story. The 24-hour city {{2}} on an invisible workforce of cleaners, drivers, bakers and security staff whose routines invert normal life. Working nights is associated with serious health {{3}}, from disrupted sleep to increased risk of certain diseases, and night workers {{4}} report feeling socially invisible: shops, clinics and banks all assume daytime hours. Some cities now appoint 'night mayors' to {{5}} for this workforce, extending transport and services into the small hours. Early evidence suggests the approach {{6}}: restaurants in one pilot city reported better staff retention after late-night bus routes were introduced. The lesson is an old one — a city's glamour depends on workers it {{7}} notices, and supporting them costs far less than {{8}} them.

gaps.explanation: 'urban success' — the noun the competition advertises; failure, decay and decline reverse it.
'depends on' = relies on the workforce; insists on demands, lectures on teaches, and intrudes on disturbs.
'serious health problems' — the plural noun; grievances are complaints, damages is a legal term, and miseries does not collocate.
'report feeling socially invisible' — the reflexive echoes the subject; 'theirselves' is not standard English, and 'one another' would make them report each other.
'speak for this workforce' — represent their interests; look for and hope for mean search and wish, and send for means summon.
'the approach works' = it is effective, as the staff-retention data shows; the negative verbs reverse the evidence.
'workers it rarely notices' — seldom; 'constantly' would contradict the invisibility point, and soon and already are not frequency adverbs.
'costs far less than ignoring them' — the gerund of neglect; missing, blaming and mocking are not the alternative to supporting.
